doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Cooking on the road and Sydney's Olympics pricing
summary: He learned to cook in motel rooms on tour, cooks Mexican and Indian food, and the talk turns to band leaders pricing New Year 2000 gigs.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I hear you’re quite a chef.

I’m an amateur chef. I started when I was on the road and the only food you could get was pretty third rate, so I started cooking for myself and the guys in the band, in the motel rooms. You know you’d drive up to a motel and the guy’d come out and he’d always give you the coffee and the milk, so you could make your own tea in the room. The first thing they do is they give you the key, and a little jug of milk, when you’d check in. And he saw all the pots and pans and he says, “Oh you’re not going to cook in there?” I said, “No, of course not.” So we’d go straight into the — you know we’d always cook in the bathroom where it was tiles and they have like an air thing, and we’d make steaks and everything. And guys would come in and eat it. I learned to cook in the motels. But I like cooking all sorts of things — Indian food, and it’s fun cooking Mexican food for people that have never had it. I mean it’s different here where they’re real connoisseurs, but over in Australia they talk about going out and having “taycos.” Because, you know, they don’t know how to pronounce it. So it’s kind of fun.
It must be hard to get some of the ingredients for some of that kind of thing. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

Yeah, it is. You have to really look. But Sydney’s pretty cosmopolitan and there’s a little pocket of Americans who’ve had a business selling, for instance, Mexican supplies, for a long time. There’s four million people now in Sydney, and they’re having the Olympics in the year 2000. So all the band leaders are thinking about, you know, what are we going to charge on New Years Eve in the year 2000, with the Olympics there? Will we start at two thousand dollars and go up? You think about these things.
You take scale, and multiply it by — let’s see —
